title: Revolutionizing drug discovery: Integrating artificial intelligence with quantitative systems pharmacology

content.abstract_summary: Critical review of AI integration within Quantitative Systems Pharmacology (QSP), covering AI-driven databases, cloud platforms, surrogate modeling, virtual patient generation, and digital twin technologies. Identifies QSP-as-a-service (QSPaaS) as an emerging model enabled by AI. Persistent challenges: computational complexity, high dimensionality, explainability, data integration, and regulatory acceptance of AI-enhanced QSP. Specifically discusses surrogate modeling (replacing computationally expensive QSP simulations with ML emulators), virtual patient generation (GAN/VAE-based synthetic populations), and digital twins linking patient-specific mechanistic models to real-time data. Authors from University of Edinburgh (Goryanin I), MMWR Ltd (Goryanin I), InSysBio CY Ltd (Demin O). Drug Discovery Today 2025.
key_findings: Surrogate modeling (emulating expensive QSP/ODE simulations with ML) is identified as the primary computational advantage AI brings to QSP — reduces evaluation cost from hours to milliseconds for virtual screening and global sensitivity analysis

Virtual patient generation via GANs, VAEs, and diffusion models enables construction of realistic synthetic patient populations for QSP simulations; addresses the small-sample QSP calibration problem by augmenting scarce clinical datasets

Digital twins (DTs) in QSP context: mechanistic QSP model personalized to individual patient data, iteratively updated as new clinical data arrives — distinguished from simpler exposure-response modeling by real-time twinning capability

QSPaaS (QSP-as-a-service): AI-enabled cloud platforms democratize QSP modeling beyond specialist groups — reduces entry barrier for smaller organizations; analogous to software services model in tech industry

Explainability is identified as a critical barrier to regulatory acceptance: black-box AI components in QSP pipelines are not acceptable to regulators without XAI methods (SHAP, attention, LIME) demonstrating mechanistic interpretability

Regulatory acceptance remains a core challenge: FDA and EMA have no specific guidance yet for AI-augmented QSP submissions; the paper calls for regulatory engagement analogous to how the field developed PBPK acceptance (now covered by ICH M15)
limitations: Review paper with no new empirical results — all claims are synthesis of existing literature, no validation experiments
Authors affiliated with commercial QSP platform (InSysBio) creating potential conflict of interest in QSPaaS advocacy
No pharmacometrics-specific methods (NONMEM, nlmixr, NLME) discussed — gap between QSP and PMx communities not bridged
Surrogate modeling accuracy vs. fidelity tradeoff not quantified — no benchmark comparisons provided for how well ML emulators replicate full QSP simulations across scenarios

extracted_claims.text: AI-driven databases and cloud-based platforms might support QSP model development and facilitate QSP as a service (QSPaaS).
Challenges such as computational complexity, high dimensionality, explainability, data integration, and regulatory acceptance persist.

Novel methodologies like surrogate modeling, virtual patient generation, and digital twin technologies [are highlighted] to enhance precision medicine, regulatory acceptability, and mechanistic interpretability.

gaps_addressed: Fills the cross-SIG (QSP×AI) positioning gap — allows MCS SIG AI WG to understand what QSP SIG is doing on AI and where MCS's mathematical rigor (UQ, identifiability) differentiates from the explainability/interpretability angle QSP uses
Surrogate modeling for QSP = the PBPK-ML emulator use case the WG has been unable to find in PubMed — this paper provides the conceptual framework even if without empirical benchmarks
Regulatory acceptance framing matches the WG's mandate: arguing that AI-augmented mechanistic models need XAI + UQ for regulatory acceptance is exactly the MCS SIG value-add over pure ML approaches
